entry.title: Implementing An RSS Feed Generator For This Site
entry.content:
I began attending IndieWebClub Bangalore meetups last month. They're fun, and I'll gush about them later. I've got a particularly hilarious comparison to make with another impressive group I've joined around the same time.

The point of this post is the work I did on the 30th of October to get included into their members directory.

Criteria

To get included on the IWCB members page, there are some criteria one has to meet:

  • Attend in-person sessions: check
  • Have a blog: check
  • Have an RSS feed on the blog: I mean… I'll implement one some dayyyy, ugh fine I'll do it now

The Thinking

Well, how tough could implementing an RSS feed be? There are probably a hundred and one plugins in Flask that'll do that for you, but I didn't want a plugin. I wanted this website to be purely handmade (well, as best as I could), so I decided to write a feed generator custom-built for my site. The way my blog was set up, I'd really have to struggle with XPath to get the feed through FreshRSS too.

So, writing a feed generator it was. Through work, I've already had experience with the BeautifulSoup library which handles HTML and XML documents. This meant I didn't have to perform string manipulation directly, which (from experience) promised to get real tiring real fast.

The feeds I already followed didn't have a common template. I know now that the difference was between Atom feeds and RSS feeds (a friend pointed out on the 3rd of November that XKCD implemented both), but I only knew RSS on the day I was motivated to implement it all.

Wikipedia listed https://www.rssboard.org/ as the official website of the RSS spec, so there I went. They had an RSS feed for their own blog linked in the sidebar. I was going to go click on it, but the link to the specification caught my eye and I had to check it out.
It was short but very dry and could not hold my attention. But wait, they linked to a page listing best practices for RSS feeds! And while this page contained more information than the spec, it's broken down into neat little sections that felt way more actionable.

The Doing

I started out with a blank Soup object

from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
soup = BeautifulSoup(features="xml")

to which I then added the top level rss tag, with the version attribute, and then the channel tag as a child tag

soup.append(soup.new_tag("rss", version="2.0))
rss = soup.rss
rss.append(rss.new_tag("channel"))

Then to the rss tag, I went about adding the metadata children tags

channel = rss.channel
for name, string in children.items:
    channel.append(channel.new_tag(name))
    channel.findall(name)[-1].string = string

This way, I could define a dictionary with the tags and their content strings to insert in one go. Of course, this meant I couldn't add any tags with attributes, but I cleverly solved that problem by not implementing any tags with attributes.

At this point, I could paste my feed in the feed validator to fix any mistakes. Finally came the item tags, each one representing one blog post. I could get all the posts from the database as a list, reverse the order (to have the recent posts at the top of the feed even though the order of the items is meaningless according to the spec), and insert the child tags for each item tag.

One thing I got lucky with was HTML escaping. To avoid confusing HTML tags and XML tags, the HTML in the blog post content must be escaped - I must use < and > instead of < and >. Thankfully, BeautifulSoup handled that implicitly for me.

The Integrating

Finally, I just set my blog up to update the feed and write it to a file every time I created, edited, or deleted a post. Then, I made the desired permanent link redirect to the static file, whose location may or may not change later.

entry.title: The slow death of a web browser
entry.content:
And the long search for a new one.

A few weeks ago, The Browser Company announced that it is shutting down Arc.

For anyone who has barely noticed, this was not a surprising update. Arc had long been on life support, receiving only security-patch updates since the company launched its second browser. Meanwhile, dozens of Arc-inspired browsers were chipping away at its once-loyal but now-infuriated customer base. The Arc-inspired dupes scene got so intense that The Browser Company ended up making Dia a dupe too.

Even though my usage of Arc paused the moment the Dia announcement dropped, the news about the browser shutting down for good brought up a lot of feelings for me. It was not a surprise, but there was also sadness for what was lost. Arc felt like the first glimpse into something truly unique and great, but also a dream that never fully manifested.

One good thing did come out of it, though. It helped move the rest of the browser industry forward. Over the last couple of years, it opened up the new possibilities of what a browser could be and challenged users to demand more of their browsers.

The browser is the most important application anyone can have on their computer. Irrespective of the work you do, you probably use one constantly. Browsers have become so capable over time that almost any task imaginable can now happen inside of a tab. Along with your regular browsing and organising your links better than ever before, you can now design, and even code in your browsers. Some are even cosplaying as full-on operating systems. Might not be the most efficient way to do something, but you still can do it!

This is why I believe everyone should care a little (a lot) more about the browser they use, probably as much as they care about the operating system on their devices.

Arc was the browser that made me care about mine. My love affair with Arc started the day I encountered those vertical tabs. Immediately, it made me reconsider what a browser could do. Other browsers had vertical tabs for a long time, but Arc’s implementation was just a little more thoughtful. With the pinned tabs and folders, it was not just another feature begrudgingly slapped onto the browser. The same held true of other features like Spaces and quick searches on other websites directly from the command bar. These were not entirely new ideas, but definitely more mindful implementations.

What made Arc such a joy to use was how it made the web feel like a place I could explore again, rather than struggle through a stream of pages, trying to pass through.

Arc’s influence is visible in other browsers today too. Despite its near-total market dominance, Chrome added features that actually make it more useful, sometimes even against the wishes of its Search team. More browsers now support tab groups and vertical tabs. Even Safari added vertical tabs. Safari, who would have thunk!

As Arc’s development slowed down, I found myself doing some intense soul-searching to find the new perfect browser for me. Around that time, nearly everyone had the same idea for what the future of browsers could be — AI. Perplexity had Comet, The Browser Company pivoted to Dia, and OpenAI, too, decided to care about browsers for a couple of weeks with Atlas. But none of them felt quite the same. After all these detours, I even went back to short stints with Vivaldi, Firefox and Chrome. Maybe lightning could strike twice?

All this searching and trying dozens of browsers, sometimes switching between multiple ones within a week, gave me a lot of clarity on what I wanted a browser to be for me.

I use my phone’s browser very differently from the one on my desktop. On my phone, it is purely a browsing and reading machine. Things like syncing, bookmarks and tab groups do not matter at all. If I want to save something, it goes to my existing workflow. My mobile browser is just a utility that comes along with me. On desktop, it is a completely different story. The browser has to feel like a home I have decorated myself. I want to keep coming back to it, find things I have stored, use them, rearrange them and explore them through a system that only makes sense to me.

I have had better luck finding a browser for my phone. Quiche has been my primary mobile browser for nearly two years now, and it has been nothing short of great. It has a clean design and snappy performance, but the best feature probably is that it does not make you think about itself. Recently, though, I upgraded to Lens, a lightweight browser that builds on many of the good ideas of Arc Search and adds some powerful developer tools on top of it. My favourite being the ability to instantly find out which fonts any webpage is using.

Meanwhile, on the desktop, I have currently given in to using Dia. Living with it for now, still asking myself whether a browser will ever make me feel the same way Arc did. Dia has also ported over many of the useful features from Arc, but what is desperately missing are fresh ideas about what a browser as an operating system could be. An idea that originated from The Browser Company in the first place. With the Atlassian acquisition, I do not know if that vision will ever come true. Or perhaps the dream is to build a Jira operating system? The horror!

Using Dia daily, I know this is not the desktop browser for me in the long term. I just do not feel the same joy I feel while using Lens, or used to with Arc. In case you have any suggestions for a good browser to explore, hit me up.

I want to ask you a few questions too. How do you browse? How do you access the internet? Is it the same across all your devices? I want you to find the perfect browser for yourself, because I believe it is the most important application on your computer.

entry.title: Super Breakfast
entry.content:
Super Breakfast

This blog is about a simple recipe which is super close to my heart.

Imagine this: you wake up on a Sunday morning starving for some good, healthy food. You have a long day ahead. First, you need to go and climb. A session can range anywhere from 5-6 hours to 10-12 hours depending on the day and mood. You'll' skip lunch cause lunch time would be just after you complete your warm-up. And regardless, you can't climb after having lunch. Your next meal you are going to have is at 21:00. You need energy to climb whole day and sustain till the evening!

If you haven't guessed it yet, this is my usual Sunday routine. To sustain this, I need a breakfast which keeps my tummy full and body brimming with energy. It definitely needs to be attractive to my taste buds and also healthy. I achieve this with a breakfast bowl, which is my take on overnight oats. It took quite a bit of experimentation and FAFO-ing to land on a recipe which ticks all the boxes.

To keep myself full, I need something which body digests slowly, solution? Oats. I add protein powder to it, and body needs some fiber to go along with it, solution? Oats. Oats add some protein to the meal themselves, so what's the best base ingredient? Oats.

I need a soaking agent(?) of sorts to soften the oats. I prefer milk. It's easier to add protein powder and fruit to it. This combination is already sweet enough, but if you are craving more sweetness, honey is a good option. I add it regardless, cause HEALTHY!!

Next up, we have peanut butter, cause who can deny more protein? More protein needs more fiber, so let's throw some basil seeds in there. That is followed by a bunch of nuts. I prefer walnuts and almonds over others.

And finally, a bunch of fruits. My usual suspects are bananas, apples and blueberries. I usually switch them with some seasonal alternatives to keep things interesting.

Here's a handy list:

  • oats
  • protein powder
  • milk
  • honey
  • peanut butter
  • nuts
  • bananas
  • apples
  • blueberries
  • basil seeds

Preparation

NOTE: Quantities reflect my preferences, change them according to your needs.

Start by adding half a litre of milk and one scoop (24g) of protein powder to a shaker. Shake aggressively till you get a smooth mixture. In the past, I used to add coffee with unflavoured protein powder. That combination works pretty well too! Now, add four tablespoon of oats to the milk base.

Next, take two to three tablespoons of peanut butter. I prefer the crunchy alternative with broken peanuts over the smooth variety. Make sure to mix the butter properly. It loves to stay with its mates, trapping oats around it and forming a weird lump. Definitely not delightful to get a full lump in the middle of mmmmmm.

Add one tablespoon of honey to it and make sure this to mix it thoroughly too. Next up, add as many nuts as you like. In the past, I have experimented with dried dates, dried figs and cashews. Sadly, none of them stuck around. I want to experiment with pumpkin seeds at some point.

Next up, we have our beloved fruits! The biggest complaint I have heard here is about bananas, some people hate how overpowering their taste is in milk. Personally, I love it. My go-to combination is half a banana, a few diced slices of apples and two or three blueberries. I stay conservative on blueberry side cause I find their taste overpowering and kinda yucky when there are too many of them in milk.

Pack everything in a jar and leave it in the fridge overnight. On the side, take a tablespoon of basil seeds and add just enough water to it. It should be just enough for basil seeds to soak it all up and become their evolved(?) version. Anything less, and they taste super weird. Anything more, and it dilutes the bowl wayyy too much. I have started using strainers recently to escape this measurement hell.

Next morning, empty the jar in a nice bowl and add the soaked basil seeds to it. Voila, we are done 🎉.

I know these photos are bad, but that's all I have right now 🙈. Maybe in my next incarnation, I'll wake up a better food blogger :P.

entry.title: What the Pho, Rosh? - Part 6
entry.content:
My Vietnam travelogue series is fondly named WTP, Rosh. You can read the fifth part here. The remaining are here.

Just as I began to protest M's suggestion of spending $250 for a Pho-kin’ visa, I heard someone call my name out loud.

“Roshni!”

I turned around. HUH? 

Why is the entrance officer at the Indian Embassy calling me?
I told M I’ll call back and hung up. As I walked towards the entrance, I asked 

“Yes sir?”

“I have a friend in Ho Chi Minh city” he started slowly. “She works at the Vietnam Immigration Department there …” Hope lit up in me and my eyes reflected it. “Oh! And will she be able to help, sir?”

He ignored my question and started narrating the story about how they became friends. I could feel Hope being nudged away by frustration and anxiety. Why is he telling me all this?

After a few minutes, but what felt like a lot more, he gave me the number of this friend and asked me to ping her with the details of M’s passport, visa and corrections required. It was 5:15 PM and all government offices shut by 5:30PM. Now, it was my turn to panic call M.

“Hello! Send your passport copy and visa immediately!”

“What.. why..Did you…”

“JUST SEND. No questions!”

“Wait, should I not go ahead with the $250 option then?”
“WHAT? NO! DON’T. JUST SEND ME THE DETAILS.”

In a minute, we sent the details to the Ho Chi Minh person. She replied five minutes later saying the details were blurry and needed a better one. 

Devre!

Another call went to M.

I still remember how M’s voice was quivering on call and how she’d said her hands were shaking and could not take a proper picture of her passport. But all said…

Our application for a new visa was made by 5:25PM. 

But we had not received a rectified visa yet. More waiting. 

It was 6PM and we still hadn’t heard anything from the Ho Chi Minh person. 

During this time, I had learnt about the entrance-officer’s life story. He was a cop in India until circumstances had him migrate. I learnt about his favourite places in Hanoi and recommendations on where to go if I craved Indian food during my stay. He even generously offered half an Indian sandwich (half a grilled sandwich with tomato chutney, peas and mashed potato cooked in Indian spices) which I gratefully took.

“Sir, doesn’t the office shut at 5:30PM?” I inquired with concern

“It shuts at 6PM, but if any applications or documents are submitted before 5:30PM, they process it the same day. If you submit it after 5:30PM, they will only process it the next day or even later. You can’t tell.”

“Oh, but we sent our details to her so close to 5:30PM.” I said without realizing I was thinking out loud.

“Yeah, let’s wait and see…”

Anxiety: Ummm…

ME: DON’T you dare!

Anxiety: But, umm..

ME: Hum, if you want. But you shan’t verbalize your concerns.

Anxiety: But if you think..

ME: Nope! Forbidden

Anxiety: ~starts making high frequency radio noises~

“Now, the window for the $250 option is also closed, by the way…” M said while waiting with me on call.

“I know, but let’s have some faith that this will go through. You start packing” I said as encouragingly as I could. Just like the wallet incident, I didn’t fully believe things would be okay. But I couldn’t let M lose hope.

6:16PM

PING!

I opened my Whatsapp and there it was - M’s visa with her name spelled correctly, with the official Vietnam Immigration Department’s letterhead. I blinked several times to verify.

Deeeeep breaths. Finally.

I heaved a big sigh of relief and sent it to M. Twelve hours later she'd land in Vietnam with no visa troubles. And she’d bring my wallet along, too. 🌚

SMH’ing to myself. Things you do for love, I say.

I thanked the entrance-officer profusely and walked to a restaurant giddy with happiness and hunger. I definitely had to have been on some Truman-show of sorts because such things happen only in the movies… Right?

Where you wait outside an Indian government office, one kind officer takes pity on your situation and decides to help you. That changes how you experience the rest of your life, and in our case, the rest of our trip.

M & I were incredibly lucky. What are the chances that I was in Vietnam when she realised the mistake? How did I just end up in front of the Indian Embassy where someone just happened to know someone?

I thanked all the stars that night and the good graces of strangers in Vietnam - Indian, Vietnamese or otherwise.

That night, on the walk back to home, is when I conceived the name for this series.

entry.title: British Politics
entry.content:
Dear Burnhamite,

You ask me what I think of British politics. Sadly, there are days when I think of nothing else. Westminster is a strange spectacle—a mob of obsequious brown-nosers with their canned-sardine jeering, with their public-school-boy humour, with their Aristotelian flights of statesmanship—that I find it hard to look away from. I am a lawyer-wonk, and there is an appeal that the New Labour era of British politics holds for a lawyer-wonk. My interest began in that era, with its dazzling characters. Tony Blair, with his force and magnetism, with his primetime great-man’ness. Gordon Brown, who Rory Stewart describes, unforgettably, as a vast spider brooding ferociously into the night.

I have a love for the West, principally for the Americans and the British. Who could resist the appeal of American mythology, which is largely true? My favourite expositor of this fact-mythology is Chinmay Ingalagavi, who also happens to be a friend:

The universities had performed miracles; there was no reason to limit them to wartime. So the post-war federal government flooded them with resources, casting them to the front lines of the Great Power competition. Public funding for research and education exploded, with the Department of Defense taking its place among the most generous patrons of scientific research in history. This concentrated the world’s best scholars to congregate in a few dozen elite universities in the United States. Transistors. Rocketry. GPS. The Internet.

The only people who could not be amazed by this are unrealists, people who have not confronted the realities of the creation of wealth. And among them are the English, who have not yet confronted the realities of their loss of wealth. As The Economist put it, ‘Britons have high expectations of a country that is far poorer than they think.’ They have the expectation that their country is a great power, without the means to sustain it. This has been exacerbated by the juvenile nature of their politics.

The Prime Ministers have been uniformly underwhelming: Cameron (mildly competent but weak), May (unlucky and weak), Johnson (strong but cretinous), Truss (insane), Sunak (sane and a quitter), Starmer (blinkered bureaucrat), and now Burnham (people-pleaser). Only Johnson, the most shameless and damaging of them, had what could be described as a forceful personality. Only Burnham seems to be capable of answering a challenge—however unseriously—at Prime Minister’s Questions, instead of retreating into a cached soundbite. The British have recently found themselves debating whether pornography of face-sitting is illegal, and whether £95 million is a reasonable price to protect bats from a railway. In Wolf Hall, Hilary Mantel’s Cromwell says ‘No ruler in the history of the world has ever been able to afford a war. They’re not affordable things.’ In Britain today, infrastructure projects are not affordable things.

There does not seem to be anything like a strategy to address the fiscal deficit, while debt financing costs are rising. In 2019–20, debt servicing was £39 billion. This year, the forecast is £124 billion. The Office for Budget Responsibility expects that figure to reach £160 billion by 2031–32. In October, the thirty-year gilt rose above 6 per cent, its highest since 1998. Their lives are becoming more expensive. Their politics focuses more and more on treats. And there seems to be less and less room for give and take; everything in British politics is a third rail.

They have been singing this tune for a long time. At the first televised debate of the House of Lords, in 1985, Lord Macmillan made a beautiful speech where he asked people to face up to the facts:

What have the Americans done? They have tackled the problem at its best. They have been the protagonists in invention, in development and in exploitation of the new technologies. They have done that on an immense scale. What is interesting is that, at the same time as all that is going on, they have reduced unemployment by means of the new wealth created. They have made 5 million new jobs altogether. […] It is the new plant, the new methods and all that goes to build them, the new wealth built ‘round them and the new service industries that have sprung up ‘round them. […] And we are somehow out of it.

Today, in the midst of the AI boom, the British are unrealists yet again. Perhaps I am a naysayer, a doomster, a wet blanket, a buzzkill. But I have little hope. Britain, in an increasingly irrevocable way, sounds like an unserious country. The British political class seems to consist, more and more, of boyband members. British politicians, from Burnham and Healey on, are understudies, ‘unrealists, illusionists playing with ideas’. These are not the men who can move the ground.

Politics is will, force, and theatre. In nationhood, I would much rather a performance of grand, serious tragedy than what seems to be a daily comedy of errors, where the players all seem to be unaware of the grand transitions taking place behind the scenes. One wishes they were merely wilfully oblivious; but one doubts they even have capacity for that lowly cynicism. The story of Thatcher and of New Labour’s Blair and Brown was a grand tragedy. Their successors seem increasingly content with farce.

The only sliver of hope is that there are no rules in politics, no regularities. Great power rivalries are random walks, and patterns can only be seen in century-view, from deathbed-view, with godlenses. From a dark decade, the Americans have proved that their soil is not quite barren, throwing up a parade of Obamas—Mamdanis, Ossoffs, El-Sayeds, Buttigiegs—of some seriousness and purpose and clarity. I hope the British too manage this someday. I hope there is still a fertile field from which new men of imagination and will might emerge, that they might face up to the electorate, dazzle them with skill and force, procure their assent—their submission—to what must be done, and drag the United Kingdom, kicking and screaming, into relevance again.

entry.title: Discovery of Emacs Features
entry.content:
• This post is my third Emacs carnival entry, this time for Nov 2026. If you're new to this site, FYI I also go by Zororg in emacs chat/universe.

I'm happy that this topic erupted after I poked around in mastodon, maybe some day I'd like to hoist as well.

Before I write up on topic, I'm sure many emacs users might remember that there was a podcast channel called "Discovering Emacs", there was a Youtube channel (rip), mastodon presence in emacs.ch (rip) and everywhere in podcast apps. It was very promising and a professional ambience to hear someone speak of dear emacs. Thankfully git repo exists, and you see the notes and how good it was, wish it had continued or someone brings similar stuff to our small church of emacs. Obviously we are ever so thankful for sacha, protesilaos and emacs-devel people for their good faith and holding up emacs for what it is today even after 50 years.

We need more community users to hold the torch, contribute, volunteer and not be behind the shiny tool-era that is making us lazy and degenerate. Me included!

Back to topic, I usually discovered emacs features based on "good to have" or "cool to have" notion and kept on exploring or adding, sooner came to realize that I've not even grossed the emacs builtins batteries. Nowadays I only discover features based on need, if not it'd be a aha/TIL moment as always.

Emacs is one best example of a perfect software for humans, and by humans. Each object or data is so well connected, that by just using emacs you keep discovering new features every now and then. The docs are the greatest feat of any software that, docs exist for humans and code exists as docs for humans too. History of emacs itself is very funny, thanks for the archives gnu mailing list has and some code has many funny comments, this all brings a smile to users at some point when they again "discover" the legacy of emacs.

Thanks to Alternate Intelligence these days that many people don't recognize the charm of emacs anymore, and thanks to the every busy world that shiny tools keep popping up to be eye candy for all. But for those who recognize or stay, surely emacs got us treat for lifetime. Emacs was almost like Second brain to many users, but now their first brain has been almost replaced by Lazy Learner’s Machine (LLM) and emacs is out of equation now.

  1. How often do you discover an Emacs feature?

    Nowadays rarely, even r/emacs has no human posts, and mastodon #emacs seems to be quite. So for now I'm just getting things done using emacs for my needs. Hopefully could find gems via mailing lists now.

  2. What was the most recent feature that you adopted?

    A consult function to change buffer font by preview. Which is very cool, just like color theme playing with different font is fun to read as per mood. Discovered via r/emacs and hackernews.

    Except for this I've been using ezemstov's fork of emacs which builds pure wayland backend using Skia GPU renderer, without GTK or cairo toolkit. Its snappier and 3-5x snappier than PGTK… read more Its even available in nix emacs-overlay (go try it out with nix shell)

  3. Are you a “Set it and forget it” type of user?

    Most config were that way, but later on trimmed them out and only keep essential ones now. Thats the reason I prefer using builtins now unless necessary. Config is now at 2K LOC.

  4. Do you read Emacs-centric social media trolling for new things to try?

    I wonder where is emacs trolling happening, but I glance actively over r/emacs and #emacs in mastodon, and obviously planet Emacs for all golden nuggets.

  5. What’s the next feature that you’d like to try?

    Canvas patch, IGC, and more than all Gnus upgrade to be async and snappier.

  6. If you’re a Feature Creator, tell us about that!

    Nope, but I've a public config that might be of interest. Also since I was missing two package needs, I tried building those (ofc with help of second brain).

    • nnflux: A Gnus backend reader for Miniflux feeds. It works like a charm with all features for RSS reading beauty.
    • denden: A ox-publish based helper tool to act as typical SSG for emacs, my site that you reading is built using that and I made it just for this purpose to replace hugo.

entry.title: Firecrackers
entry.content:
Dear Hiya,

You have asked me about firecrackers. You assert that they are bad for the environment (we agree), that they’re loud (we agree), that they’re often a nuisance (we agree), and that you want to ban them, or at least heavily tax them, or regulate them more aggressively. I know you care about air pollution and noise pollution (and everyone should read your excellent essay.)

I know you have heard of concentrated benefits and dispersed harms. Here’s Tabarrok quoting John Boehner’s memoir, On the House, where Boehner talks about how he made a wise-ass crack about the sugar industry in front of an industry lobbyist:

Without another word, I walked into my private office and shut the door. I had no real plan to go after the sugar people. I was just screwing with the guy.

My phone did not stop ringing for the next five weeks….I had no idea how many people in my district were connected to the sugar industry. People were calling all day, telling me they made pumps or plugs or boxes or some other such part used in sugar production and I was threatening their job. Mayors called to tell me about employers their towns depended on who would be hurt by a sugar downturn. It was the most organize effort I had ever seen.

And that’s why [you] don’t fuck with sugar.

Firecrackers are the motherlode of ‘concentrated benefits’ public policy stories. India is the world’s second-largest producer of firecrackers, after China. Banning them during Diwali is as bad as banning firecrackers outright, as more than 80% of sales of fireworks are concentrated around Diwali (or Deepavali, as the Tamil people call it, the relevance of which will become apparent momentarily).

More than 85% of ‘organised’ firecracker production in India comes from Sivakasi, a city in Virudhanagar District, in the State of Tamil Nadu, in the Republic of India. The fireworks industry in Sivakasi, which came out of import restrictions from the 1930s and 40s, has been enormously successful. When Nehru visited in 1960, he called it a ‘little Japan’.

Today, it brings in about $745 million in turnover every year, employs more than 300,000 people directly, and supports over 500,000 families. 70% of the workers are women. Direct jobs in fireworks manufacturing in Sivakasi are at least 4.5% of all manufacturing jobs in Tamil Nadu, and 6.5% of all female manufacturing jobs in Tamil Nadu.

May I ask you to consider Tamil Nadu politics? Seven out of 234 legislative constituencies in Tamil Nadu are in Virudhanagar, the district Sivakasi is the heart of. To make it even better, S. Keerthana, the Industries Minister of Tamil Nadu—and Industries is among the most prized of the portfolios in the Tamil Nadu Cabinet—represents Sivakasi in the Assembly, and is promising fireworks manufacturers policy changes, including to facilitate exports by moving fireworks from the “orange category” (regulated) “to white or green” (less regulated) of the pollution index.

It almost pains me to go on, but this is quite material. The present Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu, Mr Joseph C Vijay, starred in a 2005 movie, titled Sivakasi, where his name was Sivakasi. The film came out on Deepavali. Standard Fireworks, based in Sivakasi, helped sponsor it. In the movie, when a goon asks why he’s named after a town, Vijay explains that Sivakasi is where they make the fireworks, but he is where they go off. (You will not—except perhaps momentarily—regret clicking on that link.)

One last thing about Tamil Nadu. The agreement is incredibly bipartisan. When in 2021, states banned fireworks out of concern about the air pollution, the Tamil Nadu Chief Minister (then MK Stalin) wrote to four other chief ministers that “a blanket ban on firecrackers is not reasonable.” In 2026, when the new government merely inspected units after blasts, the opposition party threatened a “large-scale, democratic agitation in Sivakasi.” In 2024, the BJP’s state chief, K. Annamalai, posted a video where he said:

‘Your dear younger brother Annamalai requests you, buy a lot of crackers and burst them’ […] ‘Let us celebrate Diwali in a way our brothers and sisters in Sivakasi benefit from that.’

But my dear effective altruist, you might respond: what about the QALYs lost due to air pollution (not to mention the many many deaths that occur in Sivakasi in the course of manufacturing). You hint that, perhaps, a national government may be able to transcend these local issues. However, the BJP might end up being the greatest defender of the people of Sivakasi. They have, inexplicably, decided to make firecrackers a culture-war issue, with spokespeople saying that bans on firecrackers were ‘very anti-traditional, anti-Hindu and anti-Indian’ or ‘a conspiracy against Sanatan’ and that there would be ’no meaning to Diwali without them.’

To make things worse, here’s an article from the South China Morning Post (in 2013) stating that ‘[f]ireworks are the only component of the annual Hindu festival of lights that is yet to be taken over by the Chinese’ and that ’the attractive variety and pricing of Chinese fireworks now threaten to challenge Sivakasi’s monopoly and the livelihood of more than 750,000 people who depend on the industry.’

One cannot help but be impressed by India—this massive subcontinent—by how it can forge the most unlikely alliances, by how it belies the mildest of expectations. In this case, I am sorry to say, that coalition will be assembled firmly against you: the ‘rationalist’, ‘populist’, industrial, developmental state of Tamil Nadu will fight you tooth and nail; the right-wing, majoritarian, cultural nationalists in the BJP will fight you tooth and nail; and everyone will say we are losing to China. You will also, of course, if you win, destroy at least hundreds of businesses and hundreds of thousands of livelihoods.

I hope that hasn’t been too depressing. Eventually, I will send you letters with better news and some plans for progress. There are ways out of even the deepest of morasses. Until then, Happy Diwali!

Yours sincerely,
Nihal

entry.title: What the Pho, Rosh? - #5
entry.content:
My Vietnam travelogue series is fondly named WTP, Rosh. You can read the fourth part here. The remaining are here.

A few deep breaths and many jagged ones later

M’s flight was not until 12 hours from now. So I shut my laptop and rushed to the Indian Embassy in Hanoi. I had no plan - just some research I had done on my phone while sitting behind a Grab scooter.

I reached the Indian Embassy in Vietnam and walked towards the gate. That’s where you get stopped. You meet an officer there and if you convince him of your situation then he will ask a senior officer from within the building. If you’re visit is unplanned like mine you won’t be allowed beyond that point.

I explained my situation to the entrance-officer, showed him my research and asked him if the Embassy could help. He read my research and then called the Senior Officer wondering if the Embassy had the powers to help in such a situation.

The Senior Officer sounded confused on call and then came to the entrance. I showed him the screenshot of my research. 

He squinted at it. “Ma’am, this says Vietnam Embassy in India… not Indian Embassy in Vietnam.” I tried hiding the shock on my face as much as possible as I re-read the same screenshot. Did my brain hallucinate in panic? And how did the entrance-officer not catch this?

I tried to look sad and distraught in case that triggered some Indian-sympathy-sentiments. “Sir, Is there anything that you can do?” I pleaded with both of them.

“It’s not her fault, sir. What can she do?” I pressed

“Well, she can not board the flight and save herself from complications”, he said rudely and walked off.

As for the other officer whose job was at the entrance of the embassy - he looked at me with pity and offered me some water to drink. I thanked him for it, quietly walked not-so-far from the embassy and stood next to a tree, wondering what I could do.

Now, I really was on the verge of sad and distraught.

It was 5PM now. 10 hours to her flight. I called M and asked her if she had any luck. 

“No, none of them are answering the calls.” she said sadly, and then asked “What about with you?”

“Not yet.. But I am looking for other options. Maybe we can look at the visa on arrival option?” 

“Yeah, even that needs some prior paperwork and fee payment in advance” she said. Of course she had read through all the other alternatives in the meantime, I thought - almost smiling a sad smile to myself. “Rosh, it’s fine. I think I need to pay the $250, and I need to do that in the next hour. Else even that window will close and I will not be able to come..” 

Just as I began to protest, I heard someone call my name out loud.

“Roshni…”

I turned to see them. HUH?

Next part drops on Friday the 13th at 13:00. Stay tuned!
